title: How Does a Language Model Actually Work?
subtitle: A conceptual walkthrough for students with no prior CS background
subject: Computer Science
Mathematics
English Language Arts
summary: A jargon-free lesson that builds a working mental model of large language models using analogy, word prediction games, and a visual walkthrough. No programming knowledge required. Suitable for any class exploring AI tools.

body.text: Students are interacting with AI-powered tools daily but rarely understand what is actually happening under the hood. This lesson uses a scaffolded analogy — predicting the next word in a sentence — to build genuine intuition about how language models generate text, without requiring any background in statistics or programming.

items: Describe what a language model does in one or two plain sentences
Explain why the same prompt can produce different outputs on different runs
Identify limitations of language models that follow from how they are trained
Distinguish between what a model 'knows' and what it 'predicts'
Slide deck (linked below — editable Google Slides)
Index cards or sticky notes for the word-prediction warm-up
Optional: access to a chatbot for the live demo segment

Word prediction warm-up (10 min): Students receive sentence fragments on index cards and write the most likely next word. Class shares and votes. Introduce the concept that this is, in simplified form, what a language model does — at scale, billions of times.
Core concept slides (20 min): Walk through the slide deck covering: tokens, probability distributions, temperature, and the difference between retrieval and generation.
Live demo — prompting for surprises (10 min): Use a chatbot to show how changing a single word in a prompt shifts the output. Students predict outputs before each reveal.

Limitations gallery walk (5 min): Four posters around the room, each naming one class of language model limitation (hallucination, stale knowledge, sycophancy, context length). Students add sticky-note examples.
Exit ticket (5 min): 'Finish this sentence: A language model doesn't understand text — instead it _____.'

body.text: For advanced students: supplement with the optional reading on transformer architecture (linked below). For students who need more scaffolding: the slide deck includes an alternate 'simplified' version with fewer technical terms and more visual analogies.
